title: Regression against 2.68.1 - Grpc.Tools 2.69.0 stops working on ARM64 - Fixed in 2.83.0
body:

### What version of gRPC and what language are you using?

`2.68.1` `GrpcTools` working fine
After upgrade to `2.69.0` or `2.69.0-pre1` it is stop working


### What operating system (Linux, Windows,...) and version?

Linux Debian, eg. in [this Dockerfile](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-dotnet-instrumentation/blob/06cec4f4dc63f0a6338482b02f689828d45b9a4e/docker/debian-arm64.dockerfile).


### What runtime / compiler are you using (e.g. python version or version of gcc)

.NET9/.NET8.


### What did you do?
Please provide either 1) A unit test for reproducing the bug or 2) Specific steps for us to follow to reproduce the bug. If there’s not enough information to debug the problem, gRPC team may close the issue at their discretion. You’re welcome to re-open the issue once you have a reproduction.

### What did you expect to see?

Compilation passes/there is a documentation what was changed in this version to fix it manually.

### What did you see instead?

```log
[ERR] CompileManagedTests: /root/.nuget/packages/grpc.tools/2.69.0/build/_protobuf/Google.Protobuf.Tools.targets(291,5): error MSB6006: "/root/.nuget/packages/grpc.tools/2.69.0/tools/linux_arm64/protoc" exited with code 139. ### Anything else we should know about your project / environment?
```

Issue detected by https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-dotnet-instrumentation/pull/3926
Full build logs can be found on https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-dotnet-instrumentation/actions/runs/12914091109/job/36013613464?pr=3926 or https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-dotnet-instrumentation/actions/runs/12914091109/job/36013867300?pr=3926

### Problematic changes

I have checked couple of scenarios. Including compiling newer protobuf version on the Grpc.Tools 2.68.1 (v1.68.1 tag). It is working without any issues on Arm64.
I pretty sure that #38084 merged as 367d7e1edb98ecc064e770a065552138d7447eae leads to the problem.

comments.author: participant16
comments.body:
@participant15 I found a workaround by using a different base image:

```
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/sdk:9.0.305-bookworm-slim
RUN apt-get update && \
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends protobuf-compiler && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ENV PROTOBUF_PROTOC=/usr/bin/protoc
```

I am pretty sure just changing these in any docker file will make it work as this will make protoc use the external binary instead of the one that comes shipped with nuget

comments.body:
More details, I am not an Linux/stdlib/C++ expert but I have made some research for the root cause/potential recommendations. It will be posted in a few comments:

## Crash Analysis

### GDB Backtrace

```
Program received signal SIGSEGV, Segmentation fault.
0x0000000000917900 in ?? ()

#0  0x0000000000917900 in ?? ()
#1  0x00000000008bf8ec in ?? ()
#2  0x00000000008bf9a8 in ?? ()
#3  0x0000000000912648 in ?? ()
#4  0x00000000008e81fc in ?? ()
#5  0x0000000000420dd8 in ?? ()
#6  0x0000000000427af8 in ?? ()
#7  0x000000000042b2c4 in ?? ()
#8  0x0000000000418c14 in ?? ()
#9  0x0000fffff7d184c4 in __libc_start_call_main
#10 0x0000fffff7d18598 in __libc_start_main_impl
#11 0x0000000000417e84 in ?? ()

Backtrace stopped: previous frame identical to this frame (corrupt stack?)
```

### Crash Location Disassembly

```assembly
917900:  b8e00020    ldaddal w0, w0, [x1]    ; ARM64 LSE atomic instruction
917904:  d65f03c0    ret
917908:  2a0003f0    mov     w16, w0
91790c:  885ffc20    ldaxr   w0, [x1]
917910:  0b100011    add     w17, w0, w16
917914:  880ffc31    stlxr   w15, w17, [x1]
917918:  35ffffaf    cbnz    w15, 91790c
91791c:  d65f03c0    ret
```

The crash occurs at an **ARM64 LSE (Large System Extensions) atomic instruction** (`ldaddal`).

### Key Indicators

1. **Signal**: SIGSEGV (Segmentation Fault)
2. **Exit Code**: 139
3. **Stack State**: Corrupt - "previous frame identical to this frame"
4. **Crash Point**: In atomic operation (C++ standard library)
5. **Instruction Type**: ARM64 LSE atomic (`ldaddal`)

---

## CPU Feature Analysis

```bash
$ cat /proc/cpuinfo | grep -i "Features"
Features: fp asimd evtstrm aes pmull sha1 sha2 crc32 atomics fphp asimdhp cpuid 
          asimdrdm jscvt fcma lrcpc dcpop sha3 sm3 sm4 asimddp sha512 sve asimdfhm 
          uscat ilrcpc flagm sb paca pacg dcpodp sve2 sveaes svebitperm svesha3 
          svesm4 flagm2 frint svei8mm svebf16 i8mm bf16
```

- **CPU DOES support `atomics` (LSE)** - so the instruction itself is valid
- CPU does NOT support BTI, but binary contains BTI instructions (`bti c`)
---

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
## Comprehensive Build Infrastructure Comparison (November 6, 2025)

### Toolchain Versions

| Component | dockcross/linux-arm64 (v1.68.1) | dockcross/manylinux2014-aarch64 (v1.69.0+) |
|-----------|----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------|
| **GCC Version** | 12.3.0 (crosstool-NG 1.26.0) | 10.3.0 (crosstool-NG 1.25.0) |
| **Binutils** | 2.40 | 2.35-5.el7.4 |
| **GLIBC** | 2.36 | **2.17** ⚠️ |
| **CMake** | 3.27.5 | 3.31.5 |
| **Target Sysroot** | Debian 12 based | CentOS 7 / manylinux2014 based |

### Critical Differences

#### 1. GLIBC Version (MAJOR DIFFERENCE)
- **Old (works)**: GLIBC 2.36 (2022)
- **New (crashes)**: GLIBC 2.17 (2012) ⚠️
- **Impact**: 10-year gap in libc features, ARM64 support, and optimizations

#### 2. GCC Version  
- **Old (works)**: GCC 12.3.0 (2023)
  - Better ARM64 code generation
  - More ARM64-specific optimizations
  - Better NEON/SVE support
- **New (crashes)**: GCC 10.3.0 (2021)
  - Older ARM64 backend
  - Less mature ARM64 optimizations
  - Potentially buggy ARM64 code generation

#### 3. Compiler Configuration Differences

**dockcross/linux-arm64** (GCC 12.3.0):
```
Configured with crosstool-NG 1.26.0:
  --enable-libmudflap
  --enable-libgomp
  --disable-libquadmath
  --disable-libquadmath-support
  --disable-libsanitizer
  --disable-libmpx
  --with-tune=cortex-a72        ← ARM64 tuning
  --enable-lto
  --enable-plugin
  --enable-gold
  --disable-multilib
  --enable-long-long
  
LTO compression: zlib zstd      ← Better compression
```

**dockcross/manylinux2014-aarch64** (GCC 10.3.0):
```
Configured with crosstool-NG 1.25.0:
  --enable-cxx-flags='-I/usr/include -fpermissive'  ← Permissive mode!
  --disable-libmudflap
  --enable-libgomp
  --disable-libssp              ← Stack protection disabled!
  --disable-libquadmath
  --disable-libquadmath-support
  --disable-libsanitizer
  --disable-libmpx
  --disable-libstdcxx-verbose   ← Verbose mode disabled
  --enable-lto
  --enable-plugin
  --enable-gold
  --with-system-zlib
  --disable-multilib
  --enable-long-long
  
LTO compression: zlib only      ← No zstd support
```

#### 4. Key Build Flag Differences

| Feature | linux-arm64 | manylinux2014-aarch64 |
|---------|-------------|------------------------|
| Stack protection (SSP) | Enabled | **Disabled** ⚠️ |
| C++ flags | Standard | `-fpermissive` (relaxed) |
| libstdc++ verbose | Enabled | Disabled |
| Cortex-A72 tuning | Yes | **No** (generic ARM64) |
| LTO compression | zlib + zstd | zlib only |

### Detailed Flag Explanations

#### 1. `--disable-libssp` (Stack Smashing Protector)

**What it does**:
- SSP is a security feature that detects buffer overflows by placing "canary" values on the stack
- Before a function returns, it checks if the canary was overwritten
- If overwritten, the program terminates with SIGABRT instead of allowing exploitation

**Impact of disabling it**:
- ❌ **No stack overflow detection** - Buffer overflows go undetected
- ❌ **Less safe code** - Memory corruption bugs don't fail fast
- ❌ **Potential crash in unexpected places** - Corruption may manifest elsewhere
- ⚠️ **Could allow stack memory to be overwritten silently**, leading to:
  - Corrupted function pointers
  - Corrupted local variables
  - Segmentation faults (exit code 139) when corrupted data is used

**Why this matters for protoc crash**:
- Protobuf v29.0 uses complex ARM64 inline assembly for varint parsing
- Without SSP, stack corruption from incorrect register usage goes undetected
- Crash happens later when corrupted stack data is accessed

**Comparison**:
```
linux-arm64:         Has --enable-libssp equivalent (default)
manylinux2014:       Has --disable-libssp ⚠️ DANGEROUS
```

---

#### 2. `--enable-cxx-flags='-fpermissive'`

**What it does**:
- `-fpermissive` downgrades C++ compile errors to warnings
- Allows non-standard C++ code to compile
- Originally added to build legacy code that doesn't follow modern C++ standards

**Impact of enabling it**:
- ⚠️ **Hides real errors** - Code that should fail to compile doesn't
- ⚠️ **Undefined behavior becomes allowed** - Compiler doesn't stop you
- ⚠️ **Type safety reduced** - Invalid casts/conversions are permitted
- ⚠️ **ABI mismatches hidden** - Incompatible code links together

**Examples of what gets silently allowed**:
```cpp
// These would normally be errors, but -fpermissive allows them:
int* p = "string";              // Invalid conversion (warning only)
void func(int x);
func();                         // Missing argument (warning only)
return x;                       // Return from void function (warning only)
```

**Why this matters for protoc crash**:
- Protobuf code may have subtle type mismatches that compile anyway
- These create runtime undefined behavior
- On ARM64 with inline assembly, this can corrupt registers

**Comparison**:
```
linux-arm64:         Standard C++ strictness (errors are errors)
manylinux2014:       -fpermissive (errors become warnings) ⚠️
```

---

#### 3. `--with-tune=cortex-a72` vs generic ARM64

**What it does**:
- `--with-tune=cortex-a72` optimizes code for ARM Cortex-A72 CPU
- Cortex-A72 is a specific ARM64 processor design (used in Raspberry Pi 4, some servers)
- Generic ARM64 produces code that works on all ARM64 CPUs but is not optimized

**Impact of CPU-specific tuning**:

**Cortex-A72 tuning** (linux-arm64):
- ✅ **Instruction scheduling** optimized for Cortex-A72 pipeline
- ✅ **Branch prediction hints** tuned for Cortex-A72
- ✅ **Cache line optimizations** (Cortex-A72 has 64-byte cache lines)
- ✅ **NEON SIMD usage** optimized for Cortex-A72's NEON unit
- ✅ **Better performance** on Cortex-A72 and similar CPUs

**Generic ARM64** (manylinux2014):
- ⚠️ **Conservative instruction scheduling** (works on all, optimized for none)
- ⚠️ **Generic cache assumptions** (may miss cache optimization opportunities)
- ⚠️ **Less aggressive NEON usage** (compatibility with older ARM64)
- ⚠️ **Suboptimal on modern ARM64** (e.g., AWS Graviton, Ampere Altra)

**Why this matters for protoc crash**:
- Protobuf v29.0's ARM64 inline assembly (`VarintParseSlowArm()`) uses NEON/SIMD
- Generic tuning may generate incorrect wrapper code around inline asm
- Cortex-A72 tuning generates better code that respects inline asm constraints

**Comparison**:
```
linux-arm64:         --with-tune=cortex-a72 (optimized for specific CPU)
manylinux2014:       Generic ARM64 (no CPU tuning) ⚠️
```

---

#### 4. `--disable-libstdcxx-verbose`

**What it does**:
- Controls whether libstdc++ (C++ standard library) includes detailed diagnostics
- When enabled, exceptions and errors include more context (stack traces, locations)
- When disabled, error messages are minimal

**Impact of disabling it**:
- ❌ **Less debugging information** in exceptions
- ❌ **Harder to diagnose crashes** - No detailed stack traces
- ❌ **Silent failures** - Errors may be swallowed without clear messages

**Example**:
```cpp
// With verbose:
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'
  what():  vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 10) >= this->size() (which is 5)
  [stack trace follows]

// Without verbose:
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::out_of_range'
Segmentation fault (core dumped)
```

**Why this matters for protoc crash**:
- When protoc crashes (exit code 139 = SIGSEGV), we get no diagnostics
- With verbose mode, we might see what went wrong before the crash
- Makes debugging nearly impossible

**Comparison**:
```
linux-arm64:         Verbose mode (detailed errors)
manylinux2014:       --disable-libstdcxx-verbose (minimal errors) ⚠️
```

---

#### 5. LTO Compression: `zlib` vs `zlib + zstd`

**What it does**:
- LTO = Link-Time Optimization (optimizes across compilation units at link time)
- LTO data is compressed to reduce disk I/O during linking
- `zstd` is a newer, faster compression algorithm than `zlib`

**Impact**:
- ✅ **zstd** = Faster build times (better compression ratio, faster decompression)
- ✅ **zstd** = Smaller intermediate files during linking
- ⚠️ **zlib only** = Slower builds, larger intermediate files

**Why this matters for protoc crash**:
- ⚠️ **This likely doesn't directly cause crashes**, but:
- Older toolchain (only zlib) suggests outdated build infrastructure
- May correlate with other outdated components (GCC 10.3.0, GLIBC 2.17)

**Comparison**:
```
linux-arm64:         zlib + zstd (modern, faster)
manylinux2014:       zlib only (older, slower)
```

---

#### 6. GLIBC 2.17 vs GLIBC 2.36 (MOST CRITICAL)

**What it is**:
- GLIBC = GNU C Library (provides system calls, memory allocation, threading, etc.)
- Version 2.17 released in **December 2012** (13 years old!)
- Version 2.36 released in **August 2022** (modern)

**Impact of ancient GLIBC 2.17**:

**ARM64-specific issues**:
- ⚠️ **ARM64 was experimental in 2012** - Limited production use
- ⚠️ **Missing ARM64 syscalls** - Many added after 2.17
- ⚠️ **Buggy ARM64 assembly** in GLIBC itself (memcpy, memset, etc.)
- ⚠️ **Poor NEON/SIMD support** - ARM64 SIMD matured after 2012
- ⚠️ **Incorrect memory barrier implementations** - ARM64 threading bugs

**Modern GLIBC 2.36 improvements**:
- ✅ **10 years of ARM64 bug fixes** (2012 → 2022)
- ✅ **Optimized ARM64 assembly** for string operations
- ✅ **Better NEON/SIMD integration**
- ✅ **Complete ARM64 syscall support**
- ✅ **Fixed memory ordering bugs** on ARM64

**Why this is THE KEY ISSUE**:
- Protobuf v29.0 uses modern ARM64 features (inline assembly, NEON)
- GLIBC 2.17 doesn't properly support these features
- The binary is built against 2.17 headers/libraries
- Runtime behavior on modern systems (GLIBC 2.36+) causes mismatches
- **This is almost certainly the root cause of the crash**

**Example scenario**:
```
1. Protobuf calls memcpy() (GLIBC function)
2. Cross-compiled against GLIBC 2.17 (buggy ARM64 memcpy)
3. Binary runs on system with GLIBC 2.36
4. ABI mismatch or old buggy code path executed
5. SIGSEGV crash (exit code 139)
```

**Comparison**:
```
linux-arm64:         GLIBC 2.36 (2022, mature ARM64 support)
manylinux2014:       GLIBC 2.17 (2012, experimental ARM64) ⚠️ CRITICAL
```

---

### Summary: Combined Impact

The crash happens because **multiple weaknesses combine**:

1. **GLIBC 2.17** provides broken ARM64 foundation
2. **GCC 10.3.0** generates suboptimal ARM64 code
3. **No SSP** allows stack corruption to go undetected
4. **-fpermissive** hides compile-time errors that become runtime crashes
5. **No CPU tuning** misses optimizations that would avoid bugs
6. **No verbose errors** makes diagnosis impossible

When protobuf v29.0's optimized ARM64 assembly runs in this environment:
- It triggers edge cases in ancient GLIBC 2.17
- Stack corruption happens without detection (no SSP)
- Errors were hidden at compile time (-fpermissive)
- Code is generic and unoptimized (no tuning)
- Crash happens with no diagnostic output (no verbose)

**The fix**: Use modern toolchain (GCC 12.3+, GLIBC 2.36+) OR build natively on ARM64.

#### 5. Sysroot and ABI Differences

**dockcross/linux-arm64**:
- Based on modern Debian 12
- GLIBC 2.36 with full ARM64 support
- Modern Linux kernel headers (4.x+)
- Better ARM64 syscall support
- Modern NEON/SIMD support

**dockcross/manylinux2014-aarch64**:
- Based on CentOS 7 / RHEL 7
- **GLIBC 2.17** (ancient, limited ARM64 support)
- Old Linux kernel headers (3.x era)
- Limited ARM64 syscall support
- Older NEON/SIMD implementation

### Runtime Build Flags Comparison

When building protoc, the actual compilation commands differ:

**Common flags** (from artifact_targets.py):
```python
CXXFLAGS=""  # Empty by default
LDFLAGS=" -static-libgcc -static-libstdc++ -s"
```

**Effective flags with linux-arm64**:
```bash
# GCC 12.3 with better defaults:
- Better register allocation for ARM64
- Improved NEON vectorization
- Modern ABI compliance
- Stack protector available (even if not forced)
- Cortex-A72 tuning applied
```

**Effective flags with manylinux2014-aarch64**:
```bash
# GCC 10.3 with older defaults:
- Older ARM64 code generation
- Less aggressive NEON optimization
- Ancient GLIBC 2.17 limitations
- NO stack protector (--disable-libssp)
- Generic ARM64 (no CPU-specific tuning)
- Permissive C++ mode may hide errors
```

### Critical Analysis

**The Problem with GLIBC 2.17 (manylinux2014) on ARM64:**

1. **Timeline Issue**: GLIBC 2.17 was released in December 2012
   - ARM64 architecture was announced in October 2011
   - ARM64 was experimental/incomplete in Linux at that time
   - First ARM64 servers appeared in 2014-2015
   - Widespread ARM64 adoption started around 2017-2018

2. **Only ONE major distribution matches GLIBC 2.17**: RHEL 7 / CentOS 7
   - Released June 2014 (2+ years after GLIBC 2.17)
   - ARM64 support was **experimental** in RHEL 7
   - Known to have ARM64 bugs and limitations
   - **EOL: June 2024** ❌ - This distribution is now officially dead!

3. **ALL modern supported distributions use GLIBC 2.28+**:
   - **Ubuntu 20.04 LTS** (EOL: April 2025): GLIBC 2.31 ✅ Still supported
   - **Debian 10** (EOL: June 2024): GLIBC 2.28 ⚠️ Just reached EOL
   - **RHEL 8** (EOL: May 2029): GLIBC 2.28 ✅ Long-term support
   - All have mature, production-ready ARM64 support
   
   Older distributions (Ubuntu 16.04-18.04, Debian 9) are **all EOL** ❌

4. **Forward Compatibility**:
   - ✅ Binaries built with GLIBC 2.36 work on GLIBC 2.36+ systems
   - ⚠️ Binaries built with GLIBC 2.17 *may* work on newer systems, but:
     - Hit ABI incompatibilities with modern code
     - Trigger bugs in ancient GLIBC 2.17 ARM64 implementation
     - Miss modern syscalls and optimizations
     - **This is exactly what's happening with protoc!**

5. **Backward Compatibility Trade-off**:
   - manylinux2014 aimed for maximum compatibility (GLIBC 2.17)
   - But GLIBC 2.17's ARM64 was too immature
   - Result: Breaks on modern systems instead of helping

**Recommendation**: 
- **Minimum GLIBC for ARM64**: 2.24 (Debian 9, 2017) or 2.28 (RHEL 8, 2019)
- **Ideal GLIBC for ARM64**: 2.31+ (Ubuntu 20.04+, Debian 11+, RHEL 8+)
- This covers all production ARM64 deployments from 2019 onward
- Older systems (2014-2018) should use x86_64 or upgrade

comments.body:
The following below command was used on a Linux machine; Change this to its macOS equivalent.

1. Navigate to the C# source directory on your VM by running `cd ~/grpc/src/csharp`.
2. Create the necessary directory for the Linux aarch64 mapping by executing `mkdir -p protoc_plugins/protoc_linux_aarch64`.
3. Define your build directory by running `REAL_BUILD_DIR="../../.build_cross_arm64"`.
4. Copy the compiled protoc binary to the plugin folder with `cp -f "$REAL_BUILD_DIR/third_party/protobuf/protoc" protoc_plugins/protoc_linux_aarch64/protoc`.
5. Copy the gRPC C# plugin binary to the plugin folder with `cp -f "$REAL_BUILD_DIR/grpc_csharp_plugin" protoc_plugins/protoc_linux_aarch64/grpc_csharp_plugin`.
6. Make the copied binaries executable by running `chmod +x protoc_plugins/protoc_linux_aarch64/*`.
7. Enable compatibility for OpenSSL 3 by running `export DOTNET_SYSTEM_CRYPTO_OPENSSL_LEGACY_ALLOW=1`.
8. Configure the build to ignore other platform binaries by running `export GRPC_CSHARP_BUILD_SINGLE_PLATFORM_NUGET=1`.
9. Package the project by executing `dotnet pack Grpc.Tools/Grpc.Tools.csproj -c Release -o ../../artifacts`.
10. Verify the package creation by running `ls -lh ../../artifacts/Grpc.Tools.*.nupkg`.

comments.body:
I've hit this issue as well and have additional information that might be useful.

On arm64 (Apple Silicon / `linux/aarch64`) with Grpc.Tools **2.69–2.76** (libprotoc 29.x), I traced the `exited with code 139` (SIGSEGV) to protoc's **response-file (`@participant3`) handling** specifically, not the proto content or the spawn environment.

The same arguments crash via a response file but succeed when passed directly.

```sh
  # Crashes (139) — even with a response file containing ONLY "--version":
  printf -- '--version\n' > r.rsp
  protoc @r.rsp            # -> Segmentation fault (139)

  # Works (rc=0) — identical arg on the command line:
  protoc --version         # -> libprotoc 29.0
  ```

This matters because **MSBuild's `ProtoCompile` task always invokes `protoc @<tmp>.rsp`**, so *every* `dotnet build` crashes — but running protoc by hand (direct args) never reproduces it. That mismatch makes it look environment-specific when it isn't.

| Variable | Result |
|---|---|
| Grpc.Tools 2.68.1 / 2.67.0 (libprotoc ≤ 27.x) | works |
| Grpc.Tools 2.69.0 → 2.76.0 (libprotoc 29.x) | segfault |
| Args passed directly (no `@participant3`) | works (50/50 + under load) |
| Distro: Ubuntu 24.04 **and** Azure Linux 3.0 | both segfault |
| Independent of: env vars, signal mask, ulimits, GC mode, memory, `DOTNET_USE_POSIX_SPAWN` | still segfaults |

I worked around it by pinning Grpc.Tools to the latest working version I could find (2.68.1)

Pin the build-only tool to the last good release:

```xml
<PackageReference Include="Grpc.Tools" Version="2.68.1">
  <PrivateAssets>all</PrivateAssets>
</PackageReference>
```
